name: Narcolepsy

ethnicAssociations: Bimodal onset peak: ~15 years and ~35 years

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: ICSD-3 (International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd Edition)

criteria.description: Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) occurring daily for at least 3 months
Cataplexy (definite cataplexy with emotionally triggered episodes of sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness) - for NT1
CSF hypocretin-1 (orexin A) level <=110 pg/mL or <1/3 of normal mean - for NT1
MSLT showing mean sleep latency <=8 minutes with 2 or more sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs)
A SOREMP on the preceding nocturnal polysomnogram can replace one MSLT SOREMP

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: NT1: EDS >3 months plus either (a) definite cataplexy AND MSLT criteria, or (b) low CSF hypocretin-1. NT2: EDS >3 months plus MSLT criteria without cataplexy and without low hypocretin.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: NT1 is caused by loss of hypocretin (orexin)-producing neurons, likely autoimmune. NT2 lacks cataplexy and has normal/uncertain hypocretin levels; it may evolve into NT1. Average diagnostic delay is 8-15 years.

pathognomonic.notes: Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotions (laughter, surprise); pathognomonic for NT1; consciousness preserved
Irresistible sleep attacks; refreshing naps (typically <30 min)
REM intrusion within 15 minutes of sleep onset on MSLT

common.notes: Fragmented sleep with frequent awakenings despite EDS
Inability to move at sleep-wake transitions; may be terrifying
Vivid, often frightening visual or auditory hallucinations at sleep-wake transitions
Continuation of activities in semi-conscious state (writing nonsense, driving detours)

occasional.notes: Especially in childhood-onset NT1; related to orexin deficiency
Prolonged or recurrent cataplexy; may occur with sudden withdrawal of anticataplectics

rare.notes: In childhood-onset NT1; from hypothalamic involvement
Hypnagogic hallucinations may be misinterpreted as psychotic symptoms

rare.symptomName: Cataplexy as sole presentation in children
rare.notes: In children, cataplexy may present as hypotonic facies or tongue protrusion rather than classic falls

laboratory: CSF hypocretin-1 (orexin A) <=110 pg/mL diagnostic for NT1 (>99% specific)
CSF hypocretin-1 normal or intermediate in NT2
HLA-DQB1*06:02 present in >98% of NT1 (but also in ~25% of general population)
HLA typing supportive but not diagnostic alone
imaging: Brain MRI typically normal (used to exclude structural causes)
Research MRI: hypothalamic volume loss in NT1
MRI may show hypothalamic/brainstem lesion in secondary narcolepsy
genetic: HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele (strongest genetic risk factor; >98% of NT1 patients)
Rare autosomal dominant mutations (prepro-orexin gene extremely rare)
other: MSLT: mean sleep latency <=8 minutes with >=2 SOREMPs (preceding PSG SOREMP can count as one)
Overnight polysomnography: to exclude other sleep disorders and document SOREMP
Actigraphy: to confirm adequate sleep time before MSLT
Sleep diary for 1-2 weeks before MSLT to document adequate sleep

distinguishingFeatures: Idiopathic hypersomnia has prolonged, non-refreshing naps
Idiopathic hypersomnia has <2 SOREMPs on MSLT
Idiopathic hypersomnia has sleep drunkenness (severe sleep inertia)
OSA has apneic events on PSG (AHI >5)
OSA has snoring and witnessed apneas
OSA EDS improves with CPAP treatment
AE has cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms
Anti-IgLON5 disease can cause parasomnia and hypersomnolence

redFlags: Acute onset narcolepsy with cataplexy should raise concern for secondary cause (hypothalamic lesion, autoimmune encephalitis)
Average diagnostic delay of 8-15 years; high index of suspicion needed
Cataplexy in children may present atypically as facial hypotonia, not classic falls
Abrupt withdrawal of anticataplectic medications can trigger status cataplecticus
Narcolepsy significantly increases risk of motor vehicle accidents; driving counseling essential
H1N1 influenza and Pandemrix vaccination associated with narcolepsy onset in genetically susceptible individuals
references: Bassetti CLA, et al. Narcolepsy - clinical spectrum, aetiopathophysiology, diagnosis and treatment. Nat Rev Neurol. 2019;15(9):519-539.
Mahoney CE, et al. The neurobiological basis of narcolepsy. Nat Rev Neurosci. 2019;20(2):83-93.
American Academy of Sleep Medicine. International Classification of Sleep Disorders. 3rd ed. Darien, IL: AASM; 2014.
Liblau RS, et al. Hypocretin (orexin) biology and the pathophysiology of narcolepsy with cataplexy. Lancet Neurol. 2015;14(3):318-328.
